title: A Door Opened by the Plague
paragraphs: Between 1347 and 1352 the Black Death, carried by Genoese ships, swept across Europe, killing at least a third of its people. The human catastrophe is well documented, but historians have long been drawn to a quieter question: what happens to an economy when labour suddenly becomes scarce? With fewer hands to work the same fields, surviving peasants and labourers found themselves in an unfamiliar position of strength.

Landowners did not accept this shift quietly. In England a royal ordinance of 1349 and the Statute of Labourers passed by Parliament in 1351 tried to hold wages at the levels paid before the plague and to stop workers from leaving their employers early. Enforcement proved patchy, however, and wages for many workers rose in the decades that followed despite the law. A poll tax of 1380 helped to provoke the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

It is tempting to conclude that scarcity alone guaranteed a better life for ordinary people, yet the wider European picture complicates that story. In England, serfdom weakened over the following generations, whereas in other parts of Europe landlords later tightened their hold over peasants. Historians still debate why the same shock produced such different outcomes, and the answer may lie in the relative power of lords, towns and states in each region.

The plague, in other words, created pressure for change without dictating its direction. Demographic disaster opened a door; whether ordinary people could walk through it depended on institutions that had existed long before the first infected ships arrived.
